interactions.summary: The student reads Dante's visionary examples of wrath and Virgil's doctrinal explanation that love can be natural, rightly measured, excessive, deficient, or turned toward a bad object.
Jiang condenses Virgil's map by saying the top terraces punish forms of misguided love such as greed, gluttony, and lust.
The reading closes with Dante explicitly asking Virgil to teach him what love is.

claims.claim: Virgil's explanation in the reading says love is not automatically good: natural love is not in error, but mental love can miss by choosing evil, or by pursuing good too weakly or too strongly.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted Dante/Virgil discourse read in lecture on 2026-06-26.

claims.claim: The same discourse treats love as the seed of both virtue and punishable acts, making moral failure a distortion of the same force that can also produce good.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted Dante/Virgil discourse read in lecture on 2026-06-26.

claims.claim: Virgil names three neighbor-directed corruptions of love: seeking supremacy through another's abasement, grieving another's excellence because it threatens one's own standing, and seeking revenge for injury.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted Dante/Virgil discourse read in lecture on 2026-06-26.

claims.claim: The reading also distinguishes tepid pursuit of the good from profligate attachment to lesser goods, thereby distributing distorted love across both deficiency and excess.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted Dante/Virgil discourse read in lecture on 2026-06-26.

claims.claim: Jiang's gloss is that greed, gluttony, and lust occupy the upper terraces because they are forms of love gone astray toward the wrong object.

signature_moments.moment: Love is not merely one virtue among others but the generative seed behind both sainthood and damnable action.
signature_moments.source_phrase: love is the seed in you of every virtue and of all acts deserving punishment
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual hinge of the canto and of Jiang's broader reading of Purgatory as moral physics rather than rule-following.

signature_moments.moment: Neighbor-hating love splits into abasement, rivalry, and revenge.
signature_moments.source_phrase: ill love must mean to wish one's neighbor ill
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns sin into misdirected relational desire rather than isolated bad acts.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The deliberate, object-oriented form of love that can err by bad aim or bad measure.
Jiang's compact label for upper-terrace sins in which desire fastens onto the wrong good or loves a lesser good wrongly.

chronology_notes.note: This packet marks the lecture's shift on June 26 from writerly revelation into the central moral schema of Purgatory, where all sins are reclassified as disorders of love.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's quick terrace ordering in the spoken gloss is slightly loose, but his stable interpretive point is that the upper terraces handle excessive or misguided attachment to lesser goods.
